title: Starting a Small Business
description: Four recordings about starting a business: a radio interview with a baker, a meeting at a bank, a lecture on marketing and a talk between business partners.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A radio interview
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Lan, interviewing Marcus, who owns a bakery.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: Welcome to Business Breakfast. My guest this morning is Marcus, who opened a bakery three years ago and now has three shops. Marcus, was this always your dream?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Not at all. I trained as an engineer. I only started baking at weekends because I was stressed, and my colleagues kept asking me to bring in bread. After about a year, I realised I enjoyed that far more than my day job.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: That's quite a leap, from engineer to baker. How did you pay for it?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Partly savings, and partly a small loan from my uncle. I didn't go to a bank at first, because I couldn't show them any profits. Looking back, borrowing from family was risky, but it gave me time to learn.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: What was the hardest part?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Hours. I got up at three every morning for the first two years. And I made a classic mistake: I tried to offer thirty different products, when really we were known for just three loaves. We wasted a lot of flour.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: So what changed?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: I cut the menu to ten items and the customers actually spent more, because choosing became easier. Our profits rose by about a third within six months.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: What would you tell someone thinking of starting a business?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Test your idea cheaply before you quit your job. Sell at a market stall for a few weekends. If strangers keep coming back, you've got something.

parts.title: Part 2 · At the bank
parts.intro: You will hear a bank adviser, Mr Okoye, talking to a customer, Thu, about a loan.

script.speaker: Mr Okoye
script.text: Good morning, Miss Thu. I've read your application. You'd like to borrow five thousand pounds to start an online shop selling handmade candles. Is that right?

script.speaker: Thu
script.text: Yes, though I've been selling at craft fairs for two years, so it isn't completely new. Last year I made around four thousand pounds in sales.

script.speaker: Mr Okoye
script.text: Sales or profit?

script.speaker: Thu
script.text: Sales. After materials and stall fees, the profit was closer to one thousand five hundred.

script.speaker: Mr Okoye
script.text: Thank you for being clear. Some applicants confuse the two. Now, what would the loan be spent on?

script.speaker: Thu
script.text: About two thousand for equipment, including a bigger wax melter, one thousand for a website, and the rest for stock and advertising.

script.speaker: Mr Okoye
script.text: That seems sensible. My concern is the website. Many small businesses spend heavily on one and get few visitors. Have you considered using an existing marketplace instead?

script.speaker: Thu
script.text: I have, but the fees are high, around fifteen per cent of every sale. I'd keep more profit with my own site, and customers would remember my brand.

script.speaker: Mr Okoye
script.text: A fair argument. Here's my suggestion. I can approve three thousand now, and the remaining two thousand after six months, if your online sales reach your target.

script.speaker: Thu
script.text: That's less than I hoped for, but it's reasonable. When would I know?

script.speaker: Mr Okoye
script.text: I'll email you by Friday.

parts.title: Part 3 · A lecture on marketing
parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture by Dr Carter about marketing for small businesses.

script.speaker: Dr Carter
script.text: Good morning. Last week we looked at finance. Today we turn to a problem every small business faces: how do you get customers when you have almost no money for advertising?

script.speaker: Dr Carter
script.text: The first principle is to know exactly who your customer is. Beginners often say, my product is for everyone. In reality, that usually means it's for no one. The most successful small firms I've studied can describe a single typical customer in remarkable detail, even down to what she reads and where she shops.

script.speaker: Dr Carter
script.text: Second, use word of mouth. Research consistently shows that people trust recommendations from friends far more than any advertisement. So make it easy to recommend you. One florist I know puts a small card in every bouquet, offering ten per cent off for the recipient's friends.

script.speaker: Dr Carter
script.text: Third, be visible locally. Sponsor a school team, run a free workshop, attend community events. These cost little, yet they build trust in a way that a flashy poster never will.

script.speaker: Dr Carter
script.text: Now, a warning. Many owners spend their first month's budget on social media advertising and see no results. That doesn't mean social media is useless, but unless you've defined your customer and your message, you're simply paying to shout into a crowd.

script.speaker: Dr Carter
script.text: In next week's seminar, I'd like each of you to bring a one-page description of your ideal customer for a business of your choice.

parts.title: Part 4 · Business partners
parts.intro: You will hear two business partners, Sara and Minh, talking about their shop.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Minh, we need to talk about Saturdays. I've turned away customers three weekends in a row because we can't keep up.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: I know, and I hate it. But hiring someone is a big commitment. A part-time wage would cost us roughly eight hundred pounds a month.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: True. But think about what we're losing. If we sell even ten more orders on Saturdays, the wage pays for itself.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Hmm. Is that realistic? Those ten are probably guesses.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Not guesses. I counted. On the last Saturday, I said no to twelve people.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Twelve? You didn't tell me it was that many. OK, that changes things. But I'd rather raise our prices first. We haven't increased them in two years, and our costs have gone up.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: I'm nervous about that. Customers love us because we're affordable.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: A small increase, say five per cent, wouldn't drive anyone away. And if we're busy enough to turn people down, we're probably too cheap.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: That's a clever way of looking at it. All right. Raise prices at the start of next month, and advertise for a part-time helper at the same time.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Agreed. Let's see how it goes for three months, then review.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: And I'm drafting the advertisement tonight, so don't tell me I'm rushing.

questions.text: How did Marcus start baking?
options: He studied baking at college first
He lost his job as an engineer
He inherited a shop from his uncle
He baked at weekends to relax
questions.explanation: He began baking because he was stressed, and colleagues kept asking him to bring in bread.

evidence.quote: my colleagues kept asking me to bring in bread

questions.text: Why didn't Marcus go to a bank at first?
options: He did not trust banks with his money
He did not need any money at first
He could not show them any profits
His uncle advised him not to apply
questions.explanation: He says he could not show the banks any profits, so he borrowed from his uncle.

evidence.quote: I couldn't show them any profits

questions.text: What was the hardest part for Marcus?
options: The long hours
The cost of flour
Finding customers
Paying back his uncle
questions.explanation: He got up at three every morning for two years.

evidence.quote: I got up at three every morning

questions.text: Why did cutting the menu help?
options: It made choosing easier, so customers spent more
It allowed him to close earlier each day
It saved on rent, so he could open more shops
It attracted tourists to the new shops
questions.explanation: He says customers spent more because choosing became easier.

evidence.quote: choosing became easier

questions.text: What advice does Marcus give?
options: Offer as many different products as possible
Test your idea cheaply at a market stall
Quit your job and start straight away
Borrow money from relatives to get started
questions.explanation: He advises testing an idea cheaply before quitting your job.

evidence.quote: Test your idea cheaply before you quit your job.

options: To borrow money for an online shop
To open a savings account for stock
To pay the fees for her craft fairs
To sell her handmade candles to the bank

evidence.quote: You'd like to borrow five thousand pounds

options: About four thousand pounds from sales
About one thousand five hundred pounds
About two thousand five hundred pounds
About eight hundred pounds a month

Building her own website would be cheaper

She is disappointed but accepts the offer
She is confused about the conditions
She is angry and refuses the offer

questions.text: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: How to avoid paying tax on profits
How small firms can find customers cheaply
How to pay employees fairly and on time every month
How to design a logo for a firm
questions.explanation: The speaker asks how to get customers with almost no money for advertising.

evidence.quote: how do you get customers when you have almost no money for advertising?

Because almost everyone is too busy to shop
Because there are too many competitors for it
Because such products are always very expensive

It should be avoided by every small firm
